subject: Mathematics
title: The Prime Number Quest
hook: Raj and Meera discover which numbers stand alone and why they matter.

slides.title: The Prime Number Quest
slides.inSimpleWords: Discover the secret numbers that build all others.

slides.title: Building Blocks
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj that every number is made of prime number building blocks, like atoms in chemistry.
slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers are nature's building blocks of all numbers.

slides.title: What are Prime Numbers?
slides.storyContext: Meera defines primes: numbers greater than 1 that have exactly two divisors—1 and themselves.

points.label: Prime Number
points.text: A natural number greater than 1 with exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.

points.label: Composite Number
points.text: A natural number with more than two divisors. Example: 6 (divisors: 1, 2, 3, 6).

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes are numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves.

slides.title: Raj's Prime Hunt
slides.storyContext: Raj looks at small numbers: 2 is prime (only 1, 2 divide it). 3 is prime (only 1, 3). But 4 is not—1, 2, 4 all divide it. He realizes not all numbers are prime!

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: A prime is 'indivisible' except by itself and 1, like an atom.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes stand alone; composites break apart into smaller pieces.

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj checks if numbers are prime: Is 7 prime? Only 1 and 7 divide it—yes! Is 9 prime? 1, 3, and 9 divide it—no!

example.problem: Is 13 prime? Check all divisors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Test if only 1 and the number itself divide it.

slides.title: Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Raj breaks 12 into primes: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. He draws a tree showing how 12 splits into smaller primes.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Writing a number as a product of only prime numbers. Example: 12 = 2² × 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every number can be broken into prime number pieces.

slides.title: The Factor Tree Mystery
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj why factor trees work: start at top (composite), split into two factors, keep splitting until only primes remain. Different paths lead to same prime list!

points.label: Method
points.text: Keep dividing by smallest prime until you reach primes at every branch.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor trees always end at the same primes, no matter how you branch.

slides.title: Factor Trees
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj draw trees for different numbers, each ending in prime leaves.

example.problem: Find prime factorization of 30.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep dividing by small primes until only primes remain.

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: every number has ONE unique prime factorization, like a fingerprint.

points.label: Unique Factorization
points.text: Every composite number has exactly one prime factorization (ignoring order). Example: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 always, never another way.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each number's prime breakdown is unique and unchangeable.

slides.title: Checking Prime Factorizations
slides.storyContext: Raj verifies: 24 = 2³ × 3. Multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24. Correct!

example.problem: Verify the prime factorization of 36: 36 = 2² × 3².

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply the prime factors to verify the original number.

slides.title: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera finds the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM) using prime factors.

points.label: GCD
points.text: Greatest Common Divisor: largest number dividing both. Use shared prime factors.

points.label: LCM
points.text: Least Common Multiple: smallest number divisible by both. Use all prime factors.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the biggest shared divider, LCM is the smallest common multiple.

slides.title: Raj's Bus Problem
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera notice: bus A comes every 12 minutes, bus B every 18 minutes. When do both arrive together? They use LCM to find: every 36 minutes! For dividing 24 apples and 36 oranges equally, they use GCD = 12.

points.label: Real-World Use
points.text: LCM = when events sync. GCD = how to divide equally.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD divides fairly, LCM synchronizes repeating events.

slides.title: Finding GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Raj finds GCD and LCM of 12 and 18 using their prime factorizations.

example.problem: Find GCD and LCM of 12 and 18.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD uses only shared primes, LCM uses all primes.

image.alt: Finding GCD and LCM — Prime Time

slides.title: GCD & LCM in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Meera shows uses: GCD divides equally into groups, LCM syncs repeating events.

points.label: GCD Use
points.text: Arranging 12 apples and 18 oranges into identical baskets with no leftovers.

points.label: LCM Use
points.text: Finding when two buses (one every 12 mins, one every 18 mins) leave together.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD divides, LCM synchronizes.

slides.title: Applied GCD Problem
slides.storyContext: Raj has 24 chocolates and 36 biscuits. He wants identical gift boxes with no leftover. What's the max number of boxes?

example.problem: Find GCD(24, 36) to determine max identical boxes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCD to divide equally into maximum groups.

slides.title: Applied LCM Problem
slides.storyContext: Two lights blink: one every 12 seconds, one every 18 seconds. When do both blink together?

example.problem: Find LCM(12, 18) for synchronized blink time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use LCM to find when events repeat together.

slides.title: Sieves and Prime Patterns
slides.storyContext: Meera shows the Sieve of Eratosthenes: crossing out multiples to find all primes up to 50.

points.label: Sieve Method
points.text: Cross out all multiples of each prime to find remaining primes.

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Primes become rarer as numbers get larger, but never end.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eliminate multiples to reveal all prime numbers.

image.alt: Sieves and Prime Patterns — Prime Time

slides.title: Prime Sieve Practice
slides.storyContext: Raj uses the sieve for numbers 1-30: mark 2, cross 4,6,8...; mark 3, cross 9,15,21...; mark 5, cross 25...

example.problem: Use Sieve of Eratosthenes to find primes up to 30.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mark each prime, cross out all its multiples.

slides.title: Special Primes and Twin Primes
slides.storyContext: Meera shows patterns: 2 is the only even prime, and some primes come in pairs (5&7, 11&13, 17&19).

points.label: Even Prime
points.text: 2 is the only even prime; all other primes are odd.

points.label: Twin Primes
points.text: Pairs of primes differing by 2. Examples: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19).

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 is special—the only even prime. Twin primes come in pairs.

slides.title: Finding Twin Primes
slides.storyContext: Raj searches for twin primes up to 50. He finds: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31), (41,43).

example.problem: List all twin prime pairs less than 50.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find consecutive odd primes that differ by 2.

slides.title: Prime Power Challenge
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to find prime factorizations of 36 and 45, then their GCD.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: 36 = 2² × 3², 45 = 3² × 5. GCD = 9. Verify by division.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use prime factors to solve GCD and LCM puzzles.

slides.title: Complex Factorization Challenge
slides.storyContext: Raj tackles a harder number: factor 120 completely and express it in exponential form.

example.problem: Find the prime factorization of 120 in exponential form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break the number step by step until only primes remain.

slides.title: Prime Gaps and Distribution
slides.storyContext: Meera explains why gaps between primes vary: 2→3 (gap 1), 3→5 (gap 2), 5→7 (gap 2), 7→11 (gap 4).

points.label: Prime Gap
points.text: The difference between consecutive primes. Example: gap between 11 and 13 is 2.

points.label: Density
points.text: Primes become less frequent as numbers grow (fewer in 100-200 than in 1-100).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gaps between primes grow larger as numbers increase.

slides.title: Analyzing Prime Gaps

example.problem: Find the gap between 29 and 37.
example.solution: Primes: 29, 31, 37. Gaps are 2 and 6. Largest gap in this range is 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count how many numbers separate consecutive primes.

slides.title: Divisibility Tests for Primes
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches shortcuts to check divisibility without division: by 2 (even?), by 3 (digits sum divisible by 3?), by 5 (ends in 0 or 5?).

points.label: Quick Tests
points.text: Divisible by 2: even. By 3: digit sum divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0 or 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use quick rules to check if primes divide a number.

slides.title: Using Divisibility Tests
slides.storyContext: Raj checks 315: Ends in 5 (divisible by 5). Digits: 3+1+5=9 (divisible by 3). So 315 is divisible by 3 and 5.

example.problem: Check if 315 is divisible by 2, 3, 5, 11.
example.solution: 315 is odd (not by 2). Digits sum to 9 (divisible by 3). Ends in 5 (divisible by 5). Check 11: 3-1+5=7 (not divisible by 11).

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply quick tests instead of long division.

slides.title: Finding LCM of Three Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: find LCM of 12, 18, and 20 using prime factorization.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use highest power of each prime factor.

slides.title: Real-World Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Raj needs to pack 84 pencils and 126 erasers into identical kits. What's the maximum kit size?

example.problem: Find GCD(84, 126) for maximum kit size.
example.solution: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7, 126 = 2 × 3² × 7. GCD = 2 × 3 × 7 = 42. So 42 items per kit maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCD to find the largest equal groups.

slides.title: Goldbach's Conjecture
slides.storyContext: Meera mentions an unsolved mystery: every even number > 2 is the sum of two primes. Example: 10 = 5+5, 12 = 5+7.

points.label: Goldbach's Conjecture
points.text: Every even number greater than 2 can be expressed as the sum of two primes.

points.label: Unsolved
points.text: True for all tested numbers up to trillions, but no proof yet exists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mathematicians still wonder if every even number is two primes added.

slides.title: Prime Time Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera recap: all numbers are built from primes, factor trees show the structure, GCD/LCM solve real problems.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Every number = unique product of primes.

points.label: GCD & LCM
points.text: Essential for fractions and problem-solving.

points.label: Sieves & Patterns
points.text: Ancient method to find primes; patterns exist but primes never end.

points.label: Real Uses
points.text: Cryptography, equal distribution, synchronized events.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes are nature's number building blocks.

subject: Mathematics
title: Measuring Meera's Garden
hook: Meera plans to fence and paint her garden, learning perimeter and area.

slides.title: Measuring Meera's Garden
slides.inSimpleWords: Learn how to fence the boundary and paint the inside.

slides.title: Garden Plans
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to fence her rectangular garden and paint the ground. She needs to know how much fence (perimeter) and paint (area).
slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter measures the distance around, area measures the space inside.

slides.title: What is Perimeter?
slides.storyContext: Raj walks around Meera's garden boundary. The total distance he walks is the perimeter.

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all side lengths around a closed shape.

points.label: Units
points.text: Measured in linear units: cm, m, km, inches, feet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape.

image.alt: What is Perimeter? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Walking the Garden Edge
slides.storyContext: Raj walks 8m along one side, 5m along another, 8m on the third, and 5m on the last—that's 26m total! Meera realizes she needs 26m of fencing to go around the whole garden.

points.label: Insight
points.text: Perimeter = the complete 'path' around any closed shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trace the whole boundary—that's the perimeter.

slides.title: Perimeter of Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Meera's garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. How much fencing does she need?

example.problem: Find perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 m and width 5 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (length + width).

image.alt: Perimeter of Rectangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter of Different Shapes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices the garden border has different shapes: straight sides (rectangle), curved (circle), slanted (triangle).

points.label: Square
points.text: Perimeter = 4 × side.

points.label: Triangle
points.text: Perimeter = side₁ + side₂ + side₃.

points.label: Circle
points.text: Perimeter (circumference) = 2πr (where r is radius).

slides.inSimpleWords: Add all sides for perimeter; circle uses radius and π.

slides.title: Perimeter of Squares and Triangles
slides.storyContext: Meera marks a square flower bed (side 6m) and triangular bed (sides 5m, 6m, 7m).

example.problem: Find perimeter of a square with side 6m and a triangle with sides 5m, 6m, 7m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply for squares, add all sides for triangles.

slides.title: What is Area?
slides.storyContext: Meera measures how many square meter tiles fit in her garden. Each tile is 1m × 1m.

points.label: Area
points.text: Measure of space inside a closed shape, measured in square units.

points.label: Square Units
points.text: cm², m², km², square inches, square feet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area is how much space covers the shape.

image.alt: What is Area? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Tiling the Garden
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj lay down 1m×1m tiles in rows: 8 tiles in a row, 5 rows. That's 8×5 = 40 tiles total! Each tile is 1 square meter, so the garden is 40 square meters.

points.label: Key Idea
points.text: Area = how many unit squares fit inside the shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count the square units that cover the whole shape.

slides.title: Area of Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Meera's garden 8m × 5m is covered by 40 square tiles, each 1m × 1m.

example.problem: Find area of the same garden (8 m × 5 m).

slides.inSimpleWords: Area of rectangle = length × width.

image.alt: Area of Rectangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter vs. Area
slides.storyContext: Meera notices: two gardens with same perimeter can have different areas, and vice versa.

points.label: Same Perimeter, Different Area
points.text: 2×3 rectangle: P=10, A=6. 1×4 rectangle: P=10, A=4.

points.label: Independence
points.text: Perimeter and area are independent properties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes can have same perimeter but different areas.

slides.title: Comparing Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Raj creates two garden plans: 6m×4m and 5m×5m. Which has more fence? Which has more space?

example.problem: Compare 6m×4m rectangle (P, A) with 5m×5m square (P, A).
example.solution: Rectangle: P=20m, A=24m². Square: P=20m, A=25m². Same perimeter, square has more area!

slides.inSimpleWords: Same perimeter can yield different areas.

slides.title: Area of Other Shapes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices different garden shapes: triangular flower beds and circular fountain.

points.label: Triangle Area
points.text: Area = ½ × base × height.

points.label: Circle Area
points.text: Area = π × r² (where r is radius).

slides.inSimpleWords: Different shapes have different area formulas.

image.alt: Area of Other Shapes — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Mixed Shapes
slides.storyContext: A triangular flower bed has base 6m and height 4m. What is its area?

example.problem: Find area of triangle with base 6 m and height 4 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangle area is half of the rectangle with same base and height.

slides.title: Circle Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Meera finds a circular fountain in the center. Raj measures radius = 2m. How much rope to wrap it? How much paint for the ground?

points.label: Circumference
points.text: C = 2πr or C = πd (diameter d = 2r).

points.label: Area
points.text: A = πr².

points.label: Note on π
points.text: π ≈ 3.14 or use as symbol.

slides.inSimpleWords: Circle perimeter uses 2πr, area uses πr².

slides.title: Circle Circumference and Area
slides.storyContext: Meera's fountain: radius = 2m. How much rope? How much paint?

example.problem: Find circumference and area of a circle with radius 2m (use π ≈ 3.14).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use radius to find circumference and area of circles.

slides.title: Area of Irregular Shapes
slides.storyContext: The garden has an L-shaped section. Raj breaks it into two rectangles and adds their areas.

points.label: Composite Shapes
points.text: Break irregular shapes into simple shapes (rectangles, triangles) and add areas.

slides.inSimpleWords: Split complex shapes into simpler ones, then add areas.

slides.title: L-Shaped Area
slides.storyContext: An L-shaped garden can be split into two rectangles: 8m×3m and 5m×2m. What's the total area?

example.problem: Find area of L-shaped garden split into 8m×3m and 5m×2m rectangles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add areas of parts to get the whole.

slides.title: Parallelogram and Trapezoid Areas
slides.storyContext: Meera discovers slanted shapes: parallelograms (Area = base × height) and trapezoids (Area = ½(b₁+b₂)×h).

points.label: Parallelogram
points.text: Area = base × height (height is perpendicular to base).

points.label: Trapezoid
points.text: Area = ½ × (base₁ + base₂) × height.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slanted shapes have formulas that adjust for non-perpendicular sides.

slides.title: Parallelogram and Trapezoid Problems
slides.storyContext: Raj calculates: parallelogram with base 6m, height 4m; trapezoid with bases 5m & 7m, height 3m.

example.problem: Find area of parallelogram (base 6m, height 4m) and trapezoid (bases 5m & 7m, height 3m).
example.solution: Parallelogram: A = 6 × 4 = 24m². Trapezoid: A = ½(5+7)×3 = ½×12×3 = 18m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Use base and height for parallelograms; average bases for trapezoids.

slides.title: Garden Redesign
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to expand her garden or change its shape. Raj calculates new perimeter and area.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: If Meera makes the garden 10m × 6m, new perimeter = 32m, new area = 60 sq.m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use formulas to compare different garden sizes.

slides.title: Maximum Area Challenge
slides.storyContext: Meera has 40m of fencing. Which shape—rectangle, square, or circle—fits the most area?

example.problem: With 40m fencing, find area for square (P=40), rectangle 12×8 (P=40), and circle (P=40).
example.solution: Square (10×10): A=100m². Rectangle (12×8): A=96m². Circle (C=40, r≈6.37): A≈127.7m². Circle wins!

slides.inSimpleWords: Among same perimeter, circle has largest area.

slides.title: Fencing and Painting Budget
slides.storyContext: Fencing costs Rs. 50/m, paint costs Rs. 10/m². Meera's 8m×5m garden costs how much total?

example.problem: Calculate total cost: fencing (P=26m @ Rs.50/m) + paint (A=40m² @ Rs.10/m²).
example.solution: Fencing = 26 × 50 = Rs.1300. Paint = 40 × 10 = Rs.400. Total = Rs.1700.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use perimeter for cost of border, area for cost of inside.

slides.title: Scale and Unit Conversion
slides.storyContext: Meera's blueprint is in cm but real garden is in m. Raj converts: 1m = 100cm, so 1m² = 10,000cm².

points.label: Length Conversion
points.text: 1m = 100cm, 1km = 1000m. Perimeters scale linearly.

points.label: Area Conversion
points.text: 1m² = 10,000cm², 1km² = 1,000,000m². Areas scale by square.

slides.inSimpleWords: Length doubles means perimeter doubles; area quadruples.

slides.title: Unit Conversion Practice
slides.storyContext: Meera's blueprint: garden 40cm×25cm. Real size: 8m×5m. Verify scaling.

example.problem: If blueprint is 40cm×25cm and real is 8m×5m, what's the scale?

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare dimensions to find the scale factor.

slides.title: Mixed Shapes Garden Layout
slides.storyContext: Meera's complex garden has a rectangular section (10m×6m), semicircular flower bed (r=2m), and triangular herb garden (base 4m, height 3m). Find total area.

example.problem: Find total area: rectangle 10×6, semicircle r=2, triangle base 4 height 3.
example.solution: Rectangle: 10×6=60. Semicircle: ½π×2²≈6.28. Triangle: ½×4×3=6. Total≈72.28m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Add areas of different shapes to find total garden space.

slides.title: Real-World Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Raj discovers perimeter matters for fencing cost, area for water/fertilizer. A square uses least fence for max area!

points.label: Optimization
points.text: Among all shapes with same perimeter, a circle has max area; among polygons, a square is best.

points.label: Practical
points.text: Farmers use area for crop planning; gardeners use perimeter for fencing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and circles are nature's most efficient shapes.

slides.title: Perimeter and Area Review
slides.storyContext: Meera buys fencing (perimeter) and paint (area) for her garden.

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all sides; Rectangle = 2(l+w), Circle = 2πr.

points.label: Area
points.text: Space inside; Rectangle = l×w, Triangle = ½bh, Circle = πr².

points.label: Units
points.text: Perimeter in units (m), Area in square units (m²).

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: Same perimeter ≠ same area. Different shapes matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter fences a garden, area paints its ground.

image.alt: Perimeter and Area Review — Perimeter and Area

subject: Mathematics
title: Sharing Pizza with Fractions
hook: Raj and Meera share a pizza and learn fractions the fun way.

slides.title: Sharing Pizza with Fractions
slides.inSimpleWords: Learn how to divide a pizza fairly and understand parts.

slides.title: Pizza Division
slides.storyContext: A pizza arrives. Raj cuts it into 8 equal slices. He eats 3 slices. Meera says he ate 3/8 of the pizza.
slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole.

slides.title: Understanding Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera points out: 3 slices (numerator) out of 8 total slices (denominator).

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Top number: how many parts we have.

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Bottom number: how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

slides.inSimpleWords: Numerator is top (parts chosen), denominator is bottom (parts total).

slides.title: The Pizza Slicing Mystery
slides.storyContext: Raj wonders: when Meera cuts the same pizza into 4 slices instead of 8, does the fraction change? She explains—1/2 is 1/2, whether it's 4 slices out of 8 or 2 slices out of 4!

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: The SAME piece can be written as many different fractions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different fractions can mean the same amount of pizza.

slides.title: Reading and Writing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj how to read fractions: 3/8 is 'three-eighths', 1/2 is 'one-half', 5/6 is 'five-sixths'.

example.problem: Write and read: Raj ate 3 out of 8 slices, Meera ate 2 out of 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Say numerator, then denominator name (thirds, fourths, eighths).

slides.title: Types of Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj notices different slicing: 1/4 (one quarter), 1/2 (one half), 3/8 (three eighths), 9/8 (more than whole).

points.label: Proper Fraction
points.text: Numerator < Denominator. Less than 1. Examples: 2/5, 3/8.

points.label: Improper Fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ Denominator. At least 1. Examples: 5/5, 9/8.

points.label: Mixed Number
points.text: Whole number + proper fraction. Example: 1 3/8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proper < 1, improper ≥ 1. Mixed numbers combine whole + proper.

slides.title: Two Pizzas and One More
slides.storyContext: Raj orders 2 pizzas, and they eat 3 slices from another pizza cut into 8. That's 2 and 3/8 pizzas total! Meera shows how to convert: 2 3/8 = 19/8.

points.label: Conversion
points.text: Mixed number (whole + proper) = improper fraction (parts over denominator).

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 3/8 means 1 whole pizza plus 3 slices from another.

slides.title: Converting Between Mixed and Improper
slides.storyContext: Raj eats 1 3/8 pizzas (one and three-eighths). How many eighths total? 8/8 + 3/8 = 11/8.

example.problem: Convert 1 3/8 to improper fraction and 11/8 to mixed number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mixed = improper by multiplying whole by denominator and adding numerator.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera cuts two pizzas differently: one into 4 slices (Raj eats 2 = 2/4), another into 8 slices (Meera eats 4 = 4/8). They ate the same amount!

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Fractions that represent the same part of a whole. Example: 2/4 = 4/8.

points.label: Rule
points.text: Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different fractions can mean the same amount.

slides.title: Finding Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera shows: 2/4 = 4/8 = 6/12 all equal 1/2. Raj multiplies top and bottom by 3 to verify.

example.problem: Find three equivalent fractions for 2/5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply top and bottom by same number to get equivalent.

slides.title: Simplifying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj wonders if 6/9 can be simplified. Meera divides both by 3: 6/9 = 2/3.

points.label: Simplify
points.text: Divide numerator and denominator by their GCD to get lowest terms.

points.label: Lowest Terms
points.text: When numerator and denominator share no common factors except 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide numerator and denominator by their GCD.

slides.title: Simplifying Practice
slides.storyContext: Raj simplifies several fractions: 12/16, 15/25, 8/12.

example.problem: Simplify 12/16 to lowest terms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find GCD and divide both by it.

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: who ate more—Raj (3/8) or Meera (2/5)? They find common denominator to compare.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Larger numerator = larger fraction. 3/8 vs 4/8: 4/8 is bigger.

points.label: Different Denominators
points.text: Convert to common denominator, then compare numerators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same denominator: compare numerators. Different: find common denominator.

slides.title: Comparing Fractions with Different Denominators

example.problem: Compare 3/8 and 2/5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to common denominator, compare numerators.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj ate 1/4 pizza, Meera ate 2/4. Together they ate 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Add/subtract numerators, keep denominator: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same denominator: add/subtract tops, keep bottom same.

slides.title: Adding Same Denominator
slides.storyContext: Total eaten: Raj (3/8) + Meera (2/8) + friend (1/8) = 6/8. Simplify: 6/8 = 3/4.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add numerators when denominators match.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to add 1/3 + 1/4. Meera finds LCM(3,4) = 12: 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12, sum = 7/12.

points.label: Steps
points.text: Find LCM of denominators. Convert both to equivalent fractions. Add/subtract numerators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find common denominator using LCM before adding.

slides.title: Adding Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Meera has 1/3 pizza, Raj adds 1/4 pizza. How much total?
slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to same denominator, then add.

slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera has 3/4 pizza. She cuts it in half for dessert (multiply by 1/2). Result: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.

points.label: Multiply
points.text: Multiply numerators and denominators: (a/b) × (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d).

points.label: Divide
points.text: Multiply by reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply across; divide by flipping second fraction.

slides.title: Multiplying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera has 2/3 pizza and eats 3/4 of it. How much did she eat? 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2.

example.problem: Multiply 2/3 × 3/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply numerators, multiply denominators, simplify.

slides.title: Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj has 3/4 pizza and divides it equally among 3 friends. Each gets 3/4 ÷ 3 = 3/4 × 1/3 = 1/4.
slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the divisor, then multiply.

slides.title: Pizza Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Raj eats 3/8, Meera eats 2/8, their friend eats 1/8. What fraction remains?
slides.inSimpleWords: Use addition to find total, subtract from 1.

slides.title: Recipe Scaling
slides.storyContext: A recipe calls for 1/2 cup flour and 1/4 cup sugar. Meera wants to double it. How much of each?

example.problem: Double the recipe: 1/2 cup flour × 2 and 1/4 cup sugar × 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply recipe fractions by the scaling factor.

slides.title: Complex Fraction Operations
slides.storyContext: Raj calculates: 3/4 + 1/6 - 1/8. Find LCM and solve.

example.problem: Calculate 3/4 + 1/6 - 1/8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find LCM of all denominators, convert, then add/subtract.

slides.title: Subtracting Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Meera has 5/6 pizza, eats 1/3. How much remains? 5/6 - 1/3 = 5/6 - 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2.

example.problem: Subtract 5/6 - 1/3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find common denominator, convert, then subtract.

slides.title: Fractions Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera finish their pizza lesson, understanding fractions deeply.

points.label: Basics
points.text: Numerator (parts chosen), Denominator (total parts), Types (proper, improper, mixed).

points.label: Operations
points.text: Simplify using GCD, add/subtract/multiply/divide using common denominators or reciprocals.

points.label: Equivalence
points.text: Same part can be written many ways; always simplify to lowest terms.

points.label: Real Use
points.text: Fractions describe sharing, measuring, cooking, time, and recipes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are ways to show parts of a whole.
